verdicts.why: Plain directional adverb marking departure from a place; 'went away' says nothing about how the speaker feels about the leaving.
In 'pass away' or 'fade away' the adverb marks cessation without judging it; any euphemism belongs to the phrase, not to the word.
Describes distance in space or time and takes no side on the thing that is distant.
The neutral verb for conversing; it is the plain neighbour against which chatter, prattle and gossip are measured.
Using language at all is described here with no attitude toward the speaker or the speech.
Expressing something in speech is stated flatly; the disapproval in 'how can you talk so' comes from 'so', not from the verb.
Measures duration without judging it; whether a long period is welcome or tedious is left to the context.
Measures distance and nothing more.
The unmarked word for a dwelling, the plain neighbour of hovel and mansion.
Names the household as a unit ('keep his house') with no attitude toward its members.
A building that shelters something is named without approval or dismissal.

An intensifier of assertion; it strengthens the speaker's commitment to the statement but takes no attitude toward the thing spoken of, and the irony in 'a charming mother-in-law, indeed' is supplied by context.
'Last night' and 'last address' locate something in the immediate past with no judgement attached.
Ordinal position after all others is a plain fact of sequence.
Marking something as final says nothing about whether the ending is good or bad.
Signals that the item is unexpected on a scale, which is a matter of the speaker's expectation, not approval or contempt of the item.
Boosts a comparative ('even inferior') without adding any attitude of its own.
A concessive connective ('even when'); purely logical, no evaluation.
Wishing for an outcome is the verb's meaning, not an attitude beyond it; it neither praises nor belittles the thing hoped for.
Intending with some prospect of success ('hope to lead you to the altar') is described neutrally.
Being hopeful is a state named plainly; the word does not judge the person who hopes or what they hope for.
The most general verb of possession, empty of attitude.
Causative 'have two men-servants go with her' reports an arrangement without judging it.
Ownership stated flatly; the plain neighbour of hoard or boast.
A neutral reporting verb for a further remark, unlike snap or sneer which colour how the remark was made.
